extracted.intended_audience: general public, mathematicians, and students interested in number theory and history of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A news/feature article commemorating the 30th anniversary of Andrew Wiles' announcement of his proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, describing the history, mathematical significance, human story, and aftermath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal qualities of successful mathematicians
rubrics_metrics.description: “They have to be creative, and they have to be able to enjoy being stuck.” — perseverance, creativity, and the willingness to work on a problem for long periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights Wiles' long solitary commitment (seven years in secret) and his remark “I am not a person who gives up on a problem.” It presents perseverance and enjoyment of sustained difficulty as central traits for tackling deep problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigour and thorough checking of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: An announced proof must have its details thoroughly checked; a plausible approach is not enough if gaps remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After Wiles' 1993 announcement an error (a hole) was found which required nearly a year of work with Richard Taylor to fix. The narrative stresses that experts asked questions indicating details needed verification, and that final acceptance requires resolving such issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance measured by opening new directions
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution is significant if it ‘added a substantial amount to mathematics’ and opens new doors to further problems and theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues that solved problems usually open up other unsolved ones; Wiles’ proof opened doors on modularity and the Langlands programme, initiating further progress rather than closing a field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to broader conjectures and frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Value of a result is increased if it proves or implies a major conjecture or connects disparate areas (e.g., proving the modularity conjecture to imply Fermat’s Last Theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains the strategy: show modularity (Taniyama–Shimura–Weil conjecture) in a setting general enough to imply Fermat’s Last Theorem. It frames such structural connections (to the Langlands programme) as a major part of mathematical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate venue and community scrutiny for major announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Major mathematical announcements are typically made in research meetings where experts can immediately assess plausibility and ask probing questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles announced at the Isaac Newton Institute during a three-day programme; the article recounts the ‘electric atmosphere’ and immediate expert questioning, illustrating the role of seminars and institutes in vetting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy vs openness in research strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing to work in private or share progress is a strategic decision — privacy can protect focus, while openness invites collaboration and scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles worked alone and in secret for seven years because public attention disrupted progress; the article contrasts this with later collaboration (with Richard Taylor) required to fix the gap, showing trade-offs between solitude and community involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspirational and communicative value
rubrics_metrics.description: A major mathematical achievement has value in inspiring students and the public by attaching a human story to abstract problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes how Wiles’ story (romantic history, long commitment) and the public announcement made the mathematics accessible and compelling, attracting future researchers like Jack Thorne and influencing public perception of the field.
